newsitem.title: USA: G7 to discuss keeping economy, dollar in line.
newsitem.headline: G7 to discuss keeping economy, dollar in line.

text.p: Economic policymakers from major industrial nations meet here on Sunday to discuss ways to bring their economies into better balance and prevent currencies from getting out of whack.

The meeting of the Group of Seven nations, which is being eagerly awaited by foreign exchange traders for clues on the high-flying dollar's direction, takes place against the background of a robust world economy.

But that does not mean that there are no problems. Economic growth in the United States is arguably too fast and not sustainable in the long-run without spurring inflation. Growth in Europe and Japan, in contrast, may prove too slow.

The G7 -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- have also begun to worry that the dollar's relentless rise may be turning into too much of a good thing, setting the stage for future trade problems.
"(It) is not our economic policy to go out and seek a weak dollar," President Bill Clinton told a joint news conference on Friday with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.
"But neither do we want any other actions to have the effect of throwing the exchange rate system out of whack in order to gain undue advantage in international trade," he said.

That is what some G7 officials fear may be happening with the dollar versus the yen. The greenback has risen more than 50 percent against the Japanese currency over the past two years, dramatically boosting the competitiveness of the Asian nation's exports on world markets.
At their last meeting, in Berlin in February, G7 policymakers signalled their desire for currency market stability by saying that the excessive weakness of the dollar in the past had been corrected.
But the U.S. currency has been buoyant since then, raising questions about what, if anything, the G7 will do about that.

Norbert Walter, chief economist of Deutsche Bank, Germany's largest bank, said he does not expect any action by the G7 until the dollar rises to 1.80 marks or 130 yen. The U.S. currency closed in New York on Friday at 1.7275 marks and 126.25 yen.

The dollar's rise has been fuelled by higher U.S. interest rates which make the currency more profitable for investors to hold. The U.S. Federal Reserve raised interest rates last month for the first time in two years and is widely expected to increase them further to keep the economy from overheating.
"The economy appears to be growing at an unsustainable, above-trend rate," Fed Governor Laurence Meyer said on Thursday.
That is not the problem in continental Europe or Japan, both of which have yet to enjoy full-fledged recoveries.

Japan's Hashimoto told Clinton on Friday that Japan was determined to have a strong economic recovery led from within and not fuelled by exports. But U.S. officials are worried that a big budget squeeze by Tokyo, including a rise in its consumption tax, will have the opposite effect.

European nations are also tightening their budgets in order to meet tough fiscal criteria for inclusion in the monetary union from the outset in January, 1999. The markets have been buffeted by on-again, off-again speculation about a delay in the start-up date for the project.

Massimo Russo, a senior adviser to the International Monetary Fund, warned on Saturday against any delay in the launch of a single European currency. "We at the IMF believe a delay ... would lead to substantial dangers," he said, including turmoil in financial markets.
The G7 meeting on Sunday is taking place on the fringes of the semi-annual gathering of the IMF and the World Bank, which brings together policymakers from rich and poor nations.
Developing countries, worried about falling levels of foreign aid, were expected to call at a separate meeting on Sunday for speedy debt relief for the world's poorest nations.
